title: Using the card scraper
subtitle: How to prepare and use a card scraper for fine wood finishing
excerpt: A card scraper removes a thinner shaving than a plane and leaves a cleaner surface on figured and difficult-grain wood. It requires no sandpaper and leaves no abrasive grit in the wood pores. This technique covers the three steps: filing the edge, raising the burr, and using the scraper.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin steel plate with a turned burr edge used to take very fine shavings from a wood surface, leaving a cleaner finish than sandpaper.
The tiny rolled hook of metal at the cutting edge of a scraper or chisel, formed by the steel being rolled over on itself. The burr is what does the cutting on a card scraper.

content.text: The card scraper cuts wood with a thin curl, not dust. The cutting element is a tiny rolled

on the long edge of the steel plate, formed by burnishing the edge with a harder steel rod. When held at the right angle and pushed or pulled across the wood, the burr peels a transparent shaving that is thinner than anything a plane can produce without chatter. The result is a surface with none of the abrasive rounding of sandpaper and none of the tear-out of a plane on difficult grain.

works on wood with grain that runs in multiple directions at once. Fiddleback maple and walnut with wavy figure are typical examples, where any plane stroke tears the surface. A card scraper, cutting with a burr, handles them cleanly.

Hold the scraper in a vice or on the edge of a bench. Draw a fine flat file along the long edge of the scraper, holding the file perfectly square to the face of the scraper. The edge must be flat and square. This takes two to three strokes with a sharp file. Remove any file burr with a few strokes of a fine waterstone, keeping the scraper flat on the stone surface.

Lay the scraper flat on the bench. Rub the face of the scraper with the burnisher (a hardened steel rod) at 90 degrees to the edge, pressing firmly, three or four strokes per side. This hardens the steel at the edge. Then hold the scraper vertically in the bench vice and draw the burnisher along the edge at 5 to 10 degrees past vertical, pressing hard, three strokes on each face. This rolls the hardened steel at the edge into a tiny hook (the burr). The burr is the cutting tool.

Hold the scraper with both thumbs in the centre of one face and fingers wrapped around the back. Flex the card slightly into a gentle bow by pressing the thumbs forward. This raises the centre of the burr edge to a slight angle and prevents the corners digging in. Tilt the scraper to about 75 degrees from the work surface and push or pull in the direction of the grain. The burr should produce a thin, transparent shaving. If it produces dust, the angle needs increasing slightly; if it chatters or squeaks, the angle needs reducing.

After twenty to thirty minutes of use, the scraper will begin producing dust rather than curls and the steel will feel warm under the thumbs. The burr has rolled over and been worn away. Return to step 1 and re-file the edge. A scraper can be re-prepared in two to three minutes. The steel of a quality scraper can be filed and re-burnished many hundreds of times before the edge is too far from the face to produce a workable burr.
Too much bow: if the thumbs flex the card too far, the corners lift and the burr engages in the middle only, producing a ridge. Keep the bow minimal.
Scraper angle too low: below 60 degrees, the scraper acts as a burnisher rather than a cutter and produces a glazed surface. Increase the angle.
Hot thumbs: if the steel gets hot enough to be uncomfortable in under five minutes, the burr has already failed. Re-prepare the edge.
